opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because there's a real tension in how people frame it.

If you treat the whole LLM response as a single action, which is what a lot of the RLHF and RL-from-verifiable-rewards setups effectively do, you've got one prompt, you sample a completion, you get a scalar reward at the end, and you push up the log-probability of the whole sequence in proportion to that reward. It's a contextual bandit. The nice thing is that it's conceptually simple. You don't need a value function at every token, and you don't have to worry about bootstrapping errors compounding.

The catch is that you're assigning credit to thousands of tokens using one number. The gradient estimate for each token is extremely noisy, because most of those tokens probably had nothing to do with whether you got the answer right. Maybe one key step in the reasoning mattered and the other 2,000 tokens were filler. But the policy gradient doesn't know that. It reinforces or penalizes all of them roughly equally. So you need a lot of samples to average out the noise, and that's why methods like GRPO sample a whole group of completions per prompt and use the group mean as a baseline. That baseline is doing a lot of the variance-reduction work.

When you treat it as a genuinely multi-step problem, where each token or each reasoning step is an action in an MDP, you can in principle do much better credit assignment. You learn a value function, compute advantages per step, and say this particular step increased the probability of success and that one didn't. In classical RL, that's how you get variance down. Temporal difference methods trade variance for bias.

But in practice with LLMs, learning a good per-token value function is really hard. The state is this enormous context, and the value model is often as big as the policy. If the critic is wrong, you inject bias, and that bias can be worse than the variance you were trying to remove. That's part of why people found they could drop the critic from PPO and do fine, or even better, with group-relative baselines.

So the way I see it, the single-action view is high variance but low bias, and it works because we can throw a lot of samples at it, and because the pretrained model is already a very good prior, so you're not exploring from scratch. The multi-step view promises lower variance through better credit assignment, but only if you can get a trustworthy intermediate signal, whether a learned value function, a process reward model, or some structure in the problem that tells you which steps mattered.

I think where this gets really interesting is as horizons get longer, with agents taking hundreds of actions, calling tools, and interacting with environments over hours. There, the single-action bandit framing starts breaking down, because the variance scales with the length of the trajectory, and you can't sample enough rollouts to compensate. So I suspect we'll be forced back toward the more classical multi-step machinery. The open question is how to make value estimation reliable enough at that scale that it actually helps rather than hurts.

r001.rationale: The response discusses variance, credit assignment, and longer trajectories, but it does not attribute increased variance from multi-step decomposition to correlations between actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to think about it is: when you do RL on a language model, you have a choice about what you call an "action." You can say the whole response is one action, and the environment gives you a reward at the end, so it's basically a contextual bandit. One state, one action, one reward. Or you can say every token is an action, and the reward is sparse and only shows up at the very end, and now you have a long-horizon MDP with thousands of steps.

Mathematically those are the same objective. You're maximizing the same expected return. But the variance characteristics of your gradient estimator are completely different depending on which framing you pick.

In the bandit framing, the thing you're estimating is pretty simple. You sample a bunch of responses, score them, and the advantage is just how much better this response was than the average. The noise comes from how many samples you drew per prompt. That's it. If you draw eight or sixteen completions, your baseline is decent, and the signal is reasonably clean.

In the multi-step framing, you're trying to assign credit to each token for a reward that happens way downstream. And the problem is the per-token advantage is incredibly noisy, because the outcome of a two-thousand-token reasoning trace depends on all two thousand decisions, and you're asking "how much did token 437 contribute?" The honest answer for most tokens is "almost nothing," but your estimator doesn't know that. So it attributes essentially random credit to each one, and that noise compounds over the horizon.

That's why people reach for value functions. A learned critic is supposed to tell you, at step 437, "given where you are, how good does this look?" and that lets you compute a local advantage instead of waiting for the terminal reward. In principle that's a huge variance reduction. In practice, with LLMs, the value function is really hard to learn well. The state space is enormous, the critic is usually another model the same size as the policy, and if it's wrong, you've traded variance for bias. A bad critic can actively hurt you.

So what I think has actually happened in the field, and GRPO is kind of the canonical example, is people quietly collapsed back to the bandit view. Throw out the critic, sample a group of completions, use the group mean as your baseline, and apply that single advantage uniformly to every token in the sequence. You're giving up on fine-grained credit assignment entirely. And it turns out that's fine, because the model already has really good priors about which tokens matter. The pretrained model is doing a ton of the credit assignment for you implicitly through its representations. You just need to nudge it in the right direction at the trajectory level.

The place where this breaks down is when you genuinely need the multi-step structure. Long agentic tasks, where there's intermediate feedback from the environment, tool calls that succeed or fail, that kind of thing. There, treating it as one giant bandit action is leaving signal on the table. You have information mid-trajectory and you're not using it. So I think the interesting frontier is figuring out when you actually want to pay the variance cost of per-step credit, and when the sequence-level treatment is good enough. My intuition is that the answer is mostly about how dense your intermediate rewards are. If the environment gives you nothing until the end, bandit wins. If it talks to you along the way, you probably want to listen.

r001.rationale: The response says token-level credit estimates are noisy because many decisions contribute to the final outcome and that noise compounds over the horizon. It does not attribute the variance increase to correlations between actions.

astra-6.text:
The key question is what you’re calling an action. You can treat the entire response as one action: you sample an answer, get a reward, and increase or decrease the probability of that answer. Or you can treat each token as an action, where the state is the prompt plus everything you’ve generated so far.

If you use the same terminal reward, those formulations can give you exactly the same policy gradient. The log probability of the whole response is the sum of the log probabilities of its tokens. So calling it a single action doesn’t make the variance problem disappear. You’re still sampling this enormous object and getting one number back that tells you how good it was.

The multi-step perspective makes the credit-assignment problem explicit. Maybe one reasoning step was crucial, and everything else was irrelevant. If you give every token the same reward, you don’t distinguish those cases. A value function can help by estimating, at each prefix, how well you expect the continuation to do. Then you’re asking whether a particular action made things better or worse relative to that expectation.

But estimating that value function is itself difficult. Two prefixes that look almost identical can have very different chances of arriving at the right answer. So the tradeoff is that the multi-step formulation gives you structure you can exploit to reduce variance, but you have to learn useful intermediate predictions. The single-action formulation is simpler; it doesn’t remove the underlying credit-assignment problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses variance, token-level actions, and credit assignment, but does not attribute increased variance to correlations between actions.

sol-6.1.text:
The key question is what you’re treating as an action. If the action is the entire response, then you generate a response, get a reward, and you can think of that as a contextual bandit problem. But that action is actually composed of potentially thousands of token-level decisions.

If you view those as a sequence of actions, then you have this credit assignment problem: you get a reward at the end, and you have to figure out which decisions were responsible. The policy gradient estimator essentially takes that reward and multiplies it by the sum of the log-probability gradients for all those tokens. So a lot of decisions that may have had nothing to do with whether you succeeded are contributing noise to your update.

Calling the whole response one action doesn’t make that variance disappear. You’ve just hidden the sequence inside a very large action space. The interesting question is whether you can exploit the structure of the problem—using value estimates, for example—to tell you whether a particular continuation was better or worse than what you expected from that point. That can reduce variance, but now you have to learn those estimates accurately.

r001.rationale: The response attributes variance to irrelevant token-level decisions contributing noise to the update, but does not attribute the increase to correlations between actions.
